videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module7/lesson14.sa

Ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol have the same molar mass, and both contain an O–H group. Yet the acid boils 21 °C higher, turns blue litmus red and fizzes with baking soda. See what the carboxyl group is, how to name carboxylic acids by IUPAC rules, why their molecules pair up as hydrogen-bonded dimers, and why the charge left behind after the acid loses its proton makes it a weak acid while an alcohol is no more acidic than water. Then use sodium hydrogen carbonate to identify a carboxylic acid. Two exam-style questions at the end.

videos.title: What Limits Dengue Control? Incidence, Prevalence and Wolbachia | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.originalTitle: What Limits Dengue Control? Incidence, Prevalence and Wolbachia | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module7/lesson18.sa

In 2021, a randomised trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, found about 77% fewer dengue cases where Wolbachia mosquitoes were released. Yet 2024 set a record for dengue cases reported to WHO. Using dengue in South East Asia as the named disease, learn what incidence and prevalence mean, why we compare places with rates per 100,000, and how to read a seasonal dengue graph. Then see why immunity to one dengue serotype doesn't protect against the others, how travellers carry the virus between cities and into north Queensland, and how four conditions (virus, mosquito, warmth and water, and people) are shaped by social causes. Finally, judge the Wolbachia evidence from Yogyakarta and Cairns, and combine biological and social causes to explain why dengue control is still limited. Two exam-style questions with brief feedback.

Banana and pineapple flavourings often get their smell from esters, which can be made by joining a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. See how the two halves join and release water, how to name an ester and work back to the acid and alcohol that made it, why esters boil low and smell, why esterification stops at equilibrium, and how excess reactant raises the yield while a catalyst only makes it faster. Then follow how the ester is separated, washed, dried and distilled (and why the boiling point is only a rough check), and draw a two-step flow chart from ethanol to ethyl ethanoate. Two exam-style questions at the end.

videos.title: Disease Transmission Simulation: Trace an Epidemic Back to Its Source | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.originalTitle: Disease Transmission Simulation: Trace an Epidemic Back to Its Source | Year 12 Biology Module 7
videos.description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module7/lesson04.sa

Eight cups, one secretly "infected", three rounds of sharing, and every cup turns pink. Who started it? Design a safe classroom model of an epidemic: a hidden marker (phenolphthalein indicator and a dilute base), recorded contacts, a sample saved every round, negative and positive controls and repeat runs. Trace the source with contact tracing, plot an epidemic curve, and compare person-to-person spread with a single shared source. Model indirect contact with fluorescent powder on a door handle. Then judge what the simulation can and can't show about real disease spread. Includes a risk assessment and two exam-style questions with brief feedback.

Amines and amides both contain nitrogen, but only an amine turns red litmus blue.
